title: SN 1006 Supernova Remnant (Hubble)
caption: A filament of the SN 1006 supernova remnant, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: SN 1006, SNR 327.6+14.6 · constellation Lupus · about 6,850 light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, and the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA); Acknowledgment: W. Blair (Johns Hopkins University)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: A thin, twisting ribbon of red light drifts across a field of white stars and small orange smudges. It is a tiny piece of the remnant of SN 1006, a supernova whose light reached Earth on or around May 1, 1006 A.D., when a white dwarf nearly 7,000 light-years from us blew itself apart.

People from Africa to Europe to the Far East recorded it. Probably the brightest star humans have ever seen, it outshone Venus, showed in daylight for weeks and stayed visible without a telescope for at least two and a half years. Radio astronomers found a nearly circular ring there in the mid-1960s, and in 1976 faint visible light was reported from one filament on its northwest edge, a small part of which Hubble now shows.

The ribbon marks where the blast wave now meets very thin gas, heating hydrogen until it glows. Its brightest edges mark spots where we see the shock exactly edge-on. The explosion site lies far beyond the lower right corner, and the shock moves toward the upper left.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys imaged hydrogen light, shown in red, and Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 added blue, yellow-green and red/near-infrared exposures, shown in blue-violet, green and red-orange. The remnant itself appears only in the hydrogen filter.
understand.eye: Visible light from the filament is exceedingly faint, and its first optical detection was reported only in 1976. Part of the colour also comes from near-infrared light the eye cannot see.

explore: Today the remnant is nearly 60 light-years across and its shock still races outward at roughly 6 million miles per hour, yet years usually pass between observations before its outward motion against the background stars becomes obvious. Because SN 1006 lies more than 14 degrees from the plane of the Milky Way, few other objects get in the way. The orange smudges are distant background galaxies, and most of the white dots are stars in our own galaxy.
